utterances.text: Well, when I went to the corps command, I informed the commander of the situations I had been in, of the situations I had to deal with. Together with the monitoring mission, I tried to ensure that hostilities came to an end in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it, then, sir, that based on the information you've just given us, that General Hadzihasanovic relied on your experience and judgement, your military experience and your judgement?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- usually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that based on the importance of these various commissions and other tasks that you were assigned, that General Hadzihasanovic had delegated substantial authority to you with respect to representing him and obtaining information for him.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I would assume, then, sir, that that would be an indication that General Hadzihasanovic trusted you.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one could put it that way. General Hadzihasanovic never told me that he didn't trust me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, based on all of the events that you learned about at the joint commissions or during the time you were out in the field, you kept General Hadzihasanovic appraised of these developments to the best of your ability. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, as the deputy commander of a military organisation as large as a corps, it was part of your fundamental responsibilities and duties to be kept as fully abreast of developments as possible; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to be as well informed about the situation as possible. As deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, I was able to be present when various activities were being carried out in the field through the intermediary of the European Monitoring Mission or through UNPROFOR representatives, for example, especially in areas where there was ongoing combat, in areas where one couldn't pass through without passing through in an UNPROFOR vehicle. Well, I have also testified about this in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, would it be fair to characterise the role that you had with Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond respect to attending commission meetings or meetings sponsored by international organisations in your role as being the eyes and ears of the corps commander with respect to developments at these meetings and out in the field?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in effect, you were also kind of like a scout, if you will. You were going out to deal with problems as they arose and to try to solve those problems so the corps commander didn't have to get involved with all of them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "scout," that's perhaps a simple term. I wasn't really a scout. I was supposed to observe the situation in the field with the help of the European Monitoring Mission. I mentioned the main objective of those meetings or, rather, of the work of those joint commissions. One wouldn't say that this is the work of a scout. A scout is someone who is invisible. I was visible. A scout tries to approach the enemy, come close to the enemy. Those weren't my objectives. My objectives weren't to approach the enemy to see what the enemy was doing. I wanted to carry out the requests of the international community. I wanted to carry out what the -- I wanted to do what the international community had asked me to do at that time. I wasn't a scout. For me, a scout means something else. A soldier knows what a scout's work involves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, sir -- let me turn to documents, that is, orders sent from the 3rd Corps or reports received back to the 3rd Corps from subordinate units. As part of your duties, did you routinely or regularly review and read such documents?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really did my best given the time that I had available. I really attempted to read all the reports, but I couldn't read all of them because there were a lot of units and there were a lot of reports. I was constantly in the field, but I was familiar with the substance of the reports that would be received from the field, especially in cases where the joint commission intervened, especially in cases when the joint commission was in the field. I tried to read those reports in order to be prepared for a meeting on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, did the same go for orders sent out by the commander of the 3rd Corps to the subordinate units? Did you try to keep abreast of what orders were being sent out into the field?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried as best as I could to be informed about most of the orders. I do not exclude the possibility that an order may have escaped my attention. I would like to repeat again that there was quite a number of units, and the situation was complex, as I've already told you. We did not have any means of communication, no feedback from our subordinate units. It is a big question whether all these orders reached every single soldier in due course. I do not exclude the possibility that I did not see all the orders that were sent from the corps command to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what about the 3rd Corps war diary or war log? Did you routinely review the war diaries of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not routinely. Maybe we have different views of the meaning of the word "routine." When you say routine, what I -- how I interpret it is just to go quickly through the pages, but this is not how I approached the war diary. I did not have the time to read everything that the operations officer -- officers entered into the diary. However, in the areas that were important to me, that were interesting to me, I tried to at least read as much information as possible about those areas. It is possible that when I reviewed the diary, faced with the fact that I couldn't read everything, I skipped a thing or two. So in other words, I was not in a position to read the war diary thoroughly. In any case, I did not approach any job routinely, and that includes the reviewing of the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, based on what you've just told us, would it be fair to say that you were involved in a large number of activities but, nevertheless, you did the best you could in terms of familiarising yourself with the orders of the 3rd Corps, reports received from the subordinate units, and the 3rd Corps war diary?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I tried very hard to do precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in fact, that was of particular importance for a deputy corps commander, because one of the main reasons why there was such a position was to step in for the corps commander in the event he was absent or in the unfortunate event that he was killed in action.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Deputy corps commanders are war positions, and the duty and main missions of a deputy corps commander was precisely what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you were kept as fully informed as possible about all of the events going on within corps' area of responsibility, that would permit you to step in and assume command in a moment's notice, if absolutely necessary?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the situation was such, if the commander was not present, and in an unfortunate event that a commander was killed, then I would have had to have taken over and step in. Whether I would have been familiar with all the activities in the area of responsibility of our corps is a big question. I'm sure that on the first day, I would have had major problems, but those problems would have decreased, and I believe that the superior command would have had a say in whether I could continue performing the duties of a commander or whether I would continue being the deputy commander. I don't know what the Supreme Command would have decided, whether they would have decided for me to become an acting commander or something else, but these are just speculations. In any case, I'm a professional soldier, and I would have honoured the orders of my superior command. In any case, I would have endeavoured to command all the duties of a commander. I would have endeavoured to be abreast of all the information, all the data that I did not become familiar with up to then. I was a member of this commission, and the tasks that the corps had were tactical. They were more of a tactical nature than a strategic nature. Now that you've mentioned this, there is a lot that can be said about this topic. There are all sorts of scenarios that have to be played one against each other to see how I would have reacted in such an unfortunate event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to the actual staff of the 3rd Corps Command. In 1993, approximately how many staff members were there within the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say about the 3rd Corps staff that it was composed of officers and people who did not have any military training. Some people were attached to the chief of staff. Are you referring to the entire corps command or just the corps staff? At the head of the corps staff was the chief of staff who had his bodies. This person was an officer of the former JNA who had not completed higher military education, unlike me and the commander. There was some people who did not have any military training. I can't remember exactly how many members of corps staff there were, but I know that it was not replenished to the full strength. A corps command should have anything between 110 and 120 men. In our case, the corps was not brought to the full strength, and their professionalism and their skills are another matter. In order to perform the control and command duties, people have to be trained. In a normal situation, the chief of staff of such a corps should be a general or a staff general. We did not have anybody with such education in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. General Hadzihasanovic and myself, we didn't have that much experience in the former JNA. We were lower-ranking officers despite our education. We did not have any experience in commanding larger units. And the chief of staff who wasn't educated, given the task to command such a large unit, you can imagine what position he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you made reference to higher military education. Can you tell us what, to the best of your knowledge and recollection, what higher military education General Hadzihasanovic had completed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic told me that he had completed the command Staff College, and this education enables one to perform high-level duties in the JNA, but not the highest level duties. For the highest level duties in the former JNA you were supposed to complete the command war school which was in Belgrade. This school provided one with the theoretical knowledge to perform the highest level duties in the former JNA, duties at the corps level or operational duties at the level of the Main Staff of the former SSNO. General Hadzihasanovic had graduated from the school that allowed him to be the commander of a brigade and to subsequently be promoted. This school allowed him to be promoted but not to duties that are normally performed by a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: How frequently in -- from the formation of the corps until the time period General Hadzihasanovic left, how frequently were there meetings where the brigade commanders met with the corps commander or the deputy corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely. It depended on the situation. It is very difficult for me to remember the frequency of these meetings. We did not have regular meetings, so I can't tell you that we met every week or every month. But we did have meetings, a lot of them, quite regularly. We had regular and interim meetings. I can't tell you after such a long time how often these meetings took place. I only know that meetings did take place involving the corps commander, the brigade commanders. I myself never called a meeting of brigade commanders. However, I did attend meetings with brigade commanders. I participated actively in the work at these meetings as the deputy of corps commander. However, after such a long time it is very difficult for me to remember the frequency of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the types of issues that were discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issues varied. Mostly the commanders reported on the situation in their respective units. The corps commander informed brigade commanders about the overall situation in the territory of the entire corps. He informed brigade commanders about the requests and orders received from the superior command, the upcoming tasks, and so on and so forth. This is what took place at the so-called general meetings. However, there were the so-called extraordinary meetings which preceded particular missions, which required for all the brigade commanders to gather, or maybe only some of them. This depended on the task that we received from the superior command or on the axis where the defence had to be put up or the area where either combat operations or offensive operations were to take place, or even where an attack was to take place. I shared with you an example when the Supreme Command was to launch an offensive on a certain axis. It was up to the Supreme Command to evaluate the situation and issue orders and it was up to us to carry out such orders. In any such situation, the corps commander gathered the commanders who were active on those axes, and after such meetings written orders were issued to the commanders of these brigades to enable them to be as successful as possible in the completion of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you testified earlier in the week about a meeting where General Halilovic from the Supreme Command was at one of these meetings with the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the meeting. I have already testified about this meeting. I believe that this was around 20, 21st, or 22nd April. I can't remember exactly. However, I remember the meeting itself, because the corps command has informed us about the problem that we had already encountered in the field. I remember this meeting, which was in the corps command. It was a long meeting. It lasted up to very late in the night. I can't remember how long it lasted, but it finished very late in the evening. I can't be sure of the date. I believe it was the 20th, the 21st, or the 22nd of April, 1993. Yes, I remember the meeting well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, we may have an opportunity early next week to talk a little bit more about that meeting. I simply wanted to know if that was an example of a meeting where the brigade commanders were, or some of the brigade commanders were present at the 3rd Corps and someone was also there from the Supreme Command Staff, and I believe you've confirmed that that is in fact an example of such a meeting. Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, then. I would like to provide a comment to this. I don't know what the objective of the corps commander was when he called this meeting, but I know what was said at the meeting. The corps commander was not duty-bound to inform me as his deputy of all the things that he knew, and I myself did not have the right to demand from my superior to tell me everything that he knew. I was roughly aware of the goals of the meeting because the commander did inform me. I wouldn't go into great length at this moment since you've just told me that you want to come back to this meeting. Probably I'll be given the opportunity to provide you with some more detail at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me ask you this: Based on the information that you provided to the corps commander as well as the information he received from the subordinate units' reports and these meetings of the brigade commanders and the 3rd Corps staff, would you say that General Hadzihasanovic was fully informed and aware of the developments going on within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a very difficult thing for me to assess. I am sure that he did not know everything that was going on in the field. I'm sure he had a lot of information, but nobody was in the position to know everything that was going on in the field. A lot of things were happening. The responsibilities were huge. I've already said that communication was a major problem. We lacked professional staff to analyse reports. Sometimes reports that reached us were rather illegible because they had been composed by people who lacked skills to draft them. So I cannot confirm that the corps commander had all that information available to him. He did have information. However, I'm sure that he did not have all the information about everything that was happening in the field. He was not abreast of all the tiniest details. He, I'm sure, didn't know what was happening at any of the lines at a lower tactical level. However, when it came to the higher tactical level, I'm sure that he had all the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And of course the brigade commanders and yourself were putting the most important information forward for the corps commander's consideration so that he could take action on it. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case in principle. However, I do not exclude the possibility that a brigade commander who attended a meeting or his staff who drafted a report for the corps command was not well informed and the report did not contain all the relevant information. There were cases when brigade commanders were not fully abreast of what was going on in their respective areas of responsibility. Sometimes, due to the lack of communications, the reports did not arrive the corps commander in time. So sometimes when the corps commander drafted his report, this report did not include all of the details describing everything that was at that moment going on in, for example, a trench or on a defence position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I have two follow-up questions, sir, on what you've just been explaining to us. First of all, correct me if I'm wrong, but it would seem that one of the reasons why the corps commander would have a deputy and a staff and brigade commanders reporting to him through such a system would be to ensure that the commander has only the important information or the information the commander needs to know. Because if the corps commander were being sent information on every platoon and what every squad within what every platoon was doing, the corps wouldn't be able to function. Is that -- is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the corps commander were to have all the information about every single soldier, about whether that soldier has enough ammo, food, whether his wife was ill, then such a corps commander would have a head bigger than this building. That's why there are officers, liaison officers providing communication with the corps commander. Obviously the corps commander does not have to have all information, but there are other people in the command who evaluate the information and assess what is important for the corps commander to receive. At their level, they could unify all this information. For example, when it came to logistics, the logistics men did not inform the corps commander whether units have food or ammunition. That would have been too much of a burden for the corps commander. And if the corps commander received all that information, obviously he would not have been able to process all that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's exactly my point, sir, that the corps commander had available to him lower-level commanders, a staff, and a deputy commander who could filter the information and ensure that the commander's attention was focused on the really important issues.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In addition to a deputy, there are also assistants covering various areas. The corps duties did not rely only on two men. There was an assistant commander for logistics. He was not a staff member, but all these assistants provided the commander from -- with information pertaining to their respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you one final question about reports. Now, based on your military experience, and particularly the experience that you gained during the war, would you agree with me that sometimes combat reports, interim combat reports written and transmitted while the conflict is still going on are not as accurate as reports submitted after the conclusion of the combat and when the lower level subordinate commanders can actually figure out what was happening? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that my military experience, first in the peacetime and subsequently in the wartime are two types of experience. If you did not participate in a war, you cannot understand how different this is. This is the most complex situation that one person can find themselves in. During combat, the initial information reaches you within a certain time, and then half an hour later the situation may change completely. For example, if you have initial successes, after an hour you may suffer huge losses, and you may lose that battle. So interim reports may differ from one moment to another. In the time difference between the interim report and the final combat report the situation may differ drastically. If there are no changes, then no interim reports are sent. Then an interim report is identical to the regular combat report. I do agree that an interim report, unlike the regular report, is not that accurate. I have to point out for -- again that all the reports are sent either by communications means or by couriers. We did not have any communications means. We did not have a good courier service. The distances were large. We did not have any transportation means for the couriers to bring the reports to the corps command. So there was room for discrepancies between the interim report and the regular report. Such situations are known, and they are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that we briefly go into private session so I can put some additional questions to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I make a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think it might be best if we go back into private session, please. If it concerns that testimony, sir, I would think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we shall now resume. The Prosecution is going to continue putting questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, during 1993, would it be fair to say that if -- it was in the best interests of both sides that the HVO and the ABiH would seek to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A year is a long period of time, so you cannot say anything in general terms about the whole year, and I cannot confirm this statement for the whole year. But globally speaking, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let's turn, then, to the issue of the joint command. The purpose of establishing the joint command, or one of the main purposes of establishing it, was because it was in the best interests of the ABiH and the HVO to do so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that a year is a very broad term. I've already testified that we had intelligence showing us that the HVO and the adversary were cooperated. The BH army did not cooperate with the aggressor. Later on it was proven that this cooperation did exist between the HVO and the Serbian aggressor, because the HVO ceded their positions to the Serbian aggressor. I said that this was a very long period of time, so one cannot say in general terms that that was the case. Things were different in practice. Yes, we did try to agree. We even tried to establish joint units facing the aggressor. However, this was not possible in practical terms, and I've already testified to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At what point in time were the ABiH and the HVO trying to set up a joint command in Central Bosnia? What time period?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts in 1992. I have shared with you an example of that. There were some proposals to set up a joint command for the region of Lasva or the Lasva Valley. I said that Mr. Filip Filipovic came to the command of the regional staff. We wanted to set up a joint command with him as commander and with me as his deputy commander. However, this fell through. So the first attempts to set up a joint command happened in 1992. The next attempts were in 1993, at the highest level. As a result of that, at the corps level we appointed a joint command on paper. This was in May 1993. The headquarters of this joint command was to be in Travnik. I've testified to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you attempted to set up joint units. When was that? What time period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some attempts in 1992 to set up joint units, especially when the situation was very difficult in the defence of Jajce and in the defence of Karaula. I've already testified about that so far. However, we could not set up a joint unit that would put up joint defence against the aggressor. There were some subsequent attempts. First we had to establish a joint command, which would then result in the establishment of joint units, or at least we should have defined a common goal, which would have been a defence against the aggressor. In practice, this could never be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us also earlier this week and also earlier today about a number of joint commissions; Busovaca, Vitez. Were those joint commissions also the result of the ABiH 3rd Corps and the HVO realising that it was in their best interests to establish such commissions?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initiative was launched by the European Monitoring Mission. It was their initiative to establish a joint commission in order to put up -- to put an end to the conflict and to build trust on both sides. Before that initiative on the part of the European Monitoring Mission, we tried in a written form and in documents sent to the joint command, to avoid conflicts, but again this fell through. The joint command was established by the representatives of the European Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would the ABiH have participated in the joint commissions if it wasn't in their best interest to do so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a commission is established, obviously your interest is to achieve your goals, and I've told you what the goals of the joint commission were. If it had not been in our best interest, we would have not become members of this joint commission. We did not want to enter a conflict with the HVO. We wanted to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, now I understand that the number varied throughout 1993, but can you give us your best estimate of the strength of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH during the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command wanted to establish the corps according to the establishment order that it received from the superior command. We could not establish the corps according to the regulations on the establishment of the corps. I have used the 301st Mechanised Brigade to explain that. I told you how many tanks they had. I did not give you any detail, but I can give you now. We could not establish all the motorised brigades either. Our motorised brigades had to be transformed into mountain brigades. Some mountain brigades had to be transformed into light brigades. We could not establish the corps according to the establishment order. We tried to establish it as best as we could, however, we were not very successful. Bringing the corps up to strength was never complete. Some of the brigades were fully replenished but some were below their 50 per cent strength, or even below that. It was not so much the troops that were the problems but the arms. I told you that we had weapons for only 20 or 30 per cent of the troops, which meant that one-third of brigade was armed and two-thirds were not. You know that there was an embargo on the import of weapons into Bosnia and Herzegovina. Weapons were purchased -- were being purchased on the black market. Individuals invested their funds to purchase weapons. The 3rd Corps did not have its depot where it kept all arms. It couldn't say, well, we have mobilised people, we have given them weapons, now we can have a corps as we should have it. This was just not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again, sir. I'm not interested in the establishment strengths, I'm interested in your best estimate of the number of soldiers in the ABiH 3rd Corps in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be a hundred per cent sure of the strength, but I believe that we had between 25 and 30.000 men altogether. Certainly not more than that. I can't give you a precise number. I don't want to be faced with my statement at any possible appearance before this Trial Chamber when somebody's going to face me with a figure that I have given today. I can't be sure of the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to the number of soldiers in the HVO Central Bosnia operation zone in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you that estimate, but I believe that they were inferior with regard to the 3rd Corps. I can't give you the number. However, I did not have information about the strength of the HVO, but I believe that the number of the HVO troops was lower than the number of the BiH army troops. I don't know what the difference was. It's very difficult for me to say that at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, in order to clarify your last answer. Is it a question of you not recalling the HVO strength or is it your testimony that in 1993, you never had the intelligence about the number of troops within the HVO Central Bosnia operation zone?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we did not have reliable information about the strength of the HVO in the Central Bosnia Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say that they were inferior, were they -- I'm just trying to get a sense of your recollection, sir. If you say the ABiH 3rd Corps had 25 to 30.000 men and the HVO was inferior, did the HVO have 2.000 men, 15.000 men, 20.000 men? Can you give us a better estimate of the number of men the HVO Central Bosnia operation zone had in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that their position was inferior, I did not have such a huge difference in mind. If that had been the case, then they would have had only one brigade. I'm sure that they had about 15.000 troops at the time. When I said they were inferior, what I had in mind were -- was the number of troops. In Central Bosnia, it was not possible to mobilise a larger number of HVO troops, so that would be the inferiority that I was referring to. But it was not as drastic as you are inferring; 2.000 as opposed to 25.000. That would be drastic. That would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'd like to ask you some questions about the tempo of combat operations between the ABiH 3rd Corps and the HVO Central Bosnia operation zone units during -- let's begin with the formation of the 3rd Corps. From the formation of the 3rd Corps in November 1992 until the end of 1992, were the HVO and the ABiH engaged with each other as military opponents in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take into account the period from the moment when the corps was established in December up to the end of 1992, we did not have any armed conflicts in the area of responsibility, either of the 3rd Corps or the Central Bosnia operation zone. There were skirmishes at checkpoints, some looting, but we did not have any armed conflicts in the month of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's move, then, into 1993. In January 1993, was there armed conflict between the 3rd Corps and the HVO Central Bosnia operation zone?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can say so because, in January 1993, there were armed conflicts in Busovaca, and this was part of the Central Bosnia operation zone, as well as part of the 3rd Corps area of responsibility. However, we had a specific situation in Gornji Vakuf where combat activities started in mid-May [as interpreted] 1993. The area of Gornji Vakuf is within the operation zone of the 3rd Corps, but it was not in -- within the operation zone Central Bosnia and the HVO. Gornji Vakuf is in a different system of organisation of the HVO. As far as I can remember now, this was the area of responsibility of the North-western Herzegovina operation zone. I believe that this was its name. And I know the commander there was Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. However, if you look at the entirety of January 1993, one can say that towards the end of January, there were armed conflicts in the area of responsibility of both the military formations; namely, the HVO of Central Bosnia and the BiH army or, rather, the 3rd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 78, line 18, either I have not heard the witness properly, or there is a mistake in transcript. It says that the conflict in Gornji Vakuf was in mid-May 1993. Maybe the witness should be asked to answer this question again. Maybe the witness did say so, but I didn't hear him. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you answer this? In the transcript we had mid-May 1993. Was it in mid-May, mid-June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in mid-January 1993. If I said May, I say apologise for the slip of the tongue that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in January 1993, you've told us about conflict between the ABiH and the 3rd -- and the HVO in Busovaca and in Gornji Vakuf. Was there armed conflict between the HVO and the ABiH 3rd Corps anywhere else in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were incidents, but there were no large-scale armed conflicts. There were conflicts in Gornji Vakuf and in Busovaca in January 1993, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How about February 1993? Do you recall any periods of armed conflict between the ABiH and the HVO in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts that started in January in Gornji Vakuf never stopped. Their intensity changed. And the conflicts in the area of Busovaca municipality, which started in January and escalated in January, actually, and throughout the entire period of conflict with the HVO, which ended with the Washington agreements, there were constant fightings in that area. The intensity might have changed but there were was an ongoing fighting. In February there were combat activities in Gornji Vakuf as well as in Busovaca. Their intensity was not as prominent as at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How about March 1993? Do you recall armed conflict between units of the 3rd Corps and the HVO in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that in February and March the situation was the same. There was fighting to a greater or lesser intensity. Nothing had significantly changed. There was fighting. There was a lot of tension. The units were in a state of readiness. In those areas where there was no fighting, there were difficult situations, but there was no fighting in other areas; for example, in the areas of Busovaca and Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How about April 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, the situation changed, and an armed conflict broke out in the area of the municipality of Vitez too. The fighting there in April 1993 was real. This doesn't mean that combat ended in the municipalities of Busovaca or Gornji Vakuf. I said that right up to the Washington Agreement, there was ongoing fighting of greater or lesser intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about combat operations between the HVO and units of the 3rd Corps in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In April, there was intense fighting in the area of the municipality of Vitez. In other municipalities, the situation became more complicated. There were difficulties in other municipalities. There were incidents in Travnik, in the municipality of Travnik, or the greater area of Travnik municipality. This came to a head towards the end of May 1993. But there were small-scale conflicts in Busovaca and in Gornji Vakuf. I couldn't say that other municipalities were particularly affected by combat. There were small-scale incidents in Zepca, in Kakanj. These were incidents that were dealt with, but the most difficult situation developed in the Travnik centre. The incidents there really increased in the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in the period between January and the end of May 1993, can you tell us whether any cease-fires were in effect?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We signed a large number of cease-fires, and it's true that this took place in a short period of time, a narrow stretch of territory, but there was always fighting at the lines, and snipers were quite active, and the army was quite poorly equipped, and we sustained a lot of casualties as a result of sniper activity on the part of the HVO. And when you lose a soldier or a couple of soldiers as a result of sniper activity in a narrow area, then naturally the intensity of the fighting changes. And within the framework of your defence, you have to take positions that will enable you to mount a more effective defence. There was fighting, naturally. There wasn't such fierce fighting. It wasn't large scale, but at the lines -- well, we constantly had men at the lines. We couldn't withdraw. There were defensive forces there defending the territory, but that's what the situation was like during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, based on your experience as the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps from its formation through 1993, you were familiar with the locations of the front lines, both the Serbian front lines or the Serbian aggressor front lines, as you've put it, and the HVO lines and the lines held by units of the 3rd Corps. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, yes. I couldn't tell you about all the tactical situations, but in operational terms, I knew where the 3rd Corps units were deployed. Similarly, I had information on the deployment of HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask -- I've had what's been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 930 for identification placed on an easel. I would like to ask the witness to make a number of markings on this map. I'm not sure if we'll be able to do that with the amount of time left, but I would propose that we at least start and see how far we can get before we have to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I've placed a map here, and let me tell you that a previous witness has made some markings on the map. I would ask that you take a blue marker, since the previous witness has marked in black, and I would like you to mark, to the best of your recollection, the following: The lines separating the VRS and the ABiH, to the extent they're visible, the lines separating the ABiH and the HVO, the ABiH units within the various sectors, that is, where the various 3rd Corps units were located; and of course, if you do know where corresponding HVO units on the opposite side, on the HVO side of the line are located. And I would ask if you could do this based on the situation on the ground as of mid-June 1993. Would you be able to assist us by doing this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecution mention exhibit number, and could we be told who the witness is, if there is a date and a signature at the bottom. Well, in fact, perhaps this might be confusing for the witness. Perhaps we could be told whether the witness mentioned is our witness or a Prosecution witness, or perhaps we should cover this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, you will recall, I believe it was one of the very, very first Defence witnesses. It was Prosecution Exhibit 930 marked for identification. At the time we had the witness from the 306th Mountain Brigade testify, I indicated on the record that we might be showing the same map to other witnesses, which is why we did not tender it into evidence. I am completely fine with the notion of the current witness not having to mark the lines of the 306th, because we had a witness from that unit, and I believe it was a senior witness of that unit, who made the markings of the 306th Mountain Brigade. So if we want to just leave the 306th alone, since those are already marked on the map, that's fine. So if the witness could then, based on his knowledge as the deputy commander, if he could complete the map or complete to the best of his recollection the map, that would be fine with us, but that's -- this is a map that we've used and we did indicate that we would be asking other witnesses who would have information to make additional markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think a member of the 312th Brigade marked this map, not a member of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I stand corrected. It was the 312th Brigade. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have heard the Prosecution's question. Would it be possible for you to indicate the lines of the various parties, using this map? This would concern mid-June, that period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will mark those lines. This will take some time, given the length of the lines, given the length of the front and given the area of the zone of responsibility. This will take some time for me to mark. I can't deal with the tactical level but I can deal with the operational level. I will indicate the locations of the brigade, the areas they were engaged in, but I won't be able to locate the areas of battalion and brigade engagement. I won't be able to locate the areas of company engagement. I'll try and deal with that, but the time period is also problematic. In the month of June, the situation was difficult. The front facing the HVO in the municipality of Travnik was also opened. This is why I should be given a specific date. Was it the 15th or the 16th, or the 17th? Because in June the fighting was very intense. There was fighting in Kakanj. There was fighting in Zepca. This is a vast area. I would need officers here to draw all of this. But, Your Honours, I will try to draw these lines. I can stay on for longer today, if necessary. I will also try to indicate the sectors where the HVO was present. But could I be provided with more specific information, more specific request? Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution will certainly provide you with additional information, but we have to adjourn in five minutes' time. So there are two solutions: The general can think about this over the weekend, he can try and locate the lines, sketch them for himself, and this will make it easier for him to indicate the positions on the map on Monday. Or we could do what we did last time; a witness appeared in the afternoon and marked a map in the presence of the Defence and the Prosecution. There are two ways of proceeding. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me, with respect to the two options that the Chamber has presented us with, perhaps I could ask the witness how long he anticipates it might take him to make those markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you have any estimate of how long would it actually take you to do this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General, you've followed what's been said. There are two ways of dealing with this. You can think about the matter over the weekend, and then on Monday you could indicate the respective positions of the 306th, the Serbs, the HVO, or in the afternoon, in the presence of the registrar, Defence counsel, and the Prosecution, you could come and mark the positions on the map. In that case, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I prefer the second solution. As a soldier, I first like to finish my work and then have a rest. But I think that this would take me between an hour and two hours. I suggest that we adopt the second solution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness would prefer to mark the map in the presence of the parties. He would prefer to do this in the afternoon, after the hearing. Mr. Mundis, this is the procedure that we have already recourse to, so there is a precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will discuss this after we rise with the Defence and the court officer and work out the modalities. I did want to put one additional -- because of course I won't be communicating with the witness once we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, sir, let me -- you've said that the situation was very complex in the middle of June, and everyone in the courtroom is very much aware that there was a high degree of combat activities during the early part of June or the first half of June. When did those combat operations more or less cease and the situation stabilise?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat activities did not come to an end until the Washington Agreement. When the situation, when the conflict escalated in Zepca, that was at the end of June 1993. Well, at that time, the combat activities between the army and the BH -- between the army and the HVO in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps hadn't come to an end, and this was the case right up until the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If that's the case, sir, and the confrontation lines did not stabilise in June of 1993, then I would suggest that you pick the 20th of June, 1993, as the date that you use to try to draw the lines to the best of your recollection. And we'll give you an opportunity on Monday, if there are certain areas along the line or within the area of responsibility where the situation was extremely unstable in June of 1993, we'll give you an opportunity to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the Prosecution would like you to mark the lines as they were on the 20th of June. I'm now addressing the Defence to hear what their position is with regard to the witness's desire to mark the positions. And this will take him an hour or two. This will require your presence, but naturally the witness will not be allowed to discuss matters with either of the parties as he's taken the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we agree that it is the Prosecution conducting their cross-examination now, and we'll accept the suggestion after having discussed the matter with the Prosecution. I know what the witness suggested as far as the Defence is concerned. From 1530 until 5.30 we have certain duties, but we could be present, someone could be present when the witness marks the map. We'll see how we can proceed most efficiently to obtain the result the Prosecution wants to obtain, but I don't think the task has been specified sufficiently. All we know is the date that the Prosecution has referred to, the 20th of June. We'd like to know whether the Prosecution will be requesting that all the positions of the army and the HVO be marked throughout the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. This is an additional factor that might enable us to follow the lines the witness marks, so we need to know not only about the dates but the exact positions that the witness will be asked to mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of your suggestions, Your Honours, I think it would be best to do this on Monday before the hearing, and this would give the witness some time to prepare, and it would be possible for the Defence to also be present when these positions are marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Kubura's Defence would prefer this to be done on Monday before the hearing. The registrar says that's not a bad idea. I don't know what the Prosecution position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to doing it today, tomorrow, Sunday, Monday. The witness could take the map away with him to the hotel and do it. We're indifferent as to how that needs to be done, but I do want, in light of the comments of my learned colleague from the Hadzihasanovic team, to -- I believe I did indicate exactly what I wanted the witness to do, but let me do that again for the benefit of the witness to ensure that he has no questions about what it is we want him to mark on the map, and I will try to do this as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what we're asking you -- what I'm asking you to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The witness wants a pen to make a note of what you're saying. Mr. Registrar, could we have a sheet of paper and a pen, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, what we would like you to do is, again, on the 20th of June, 1993, the situation as it existed on the ground as depicted on this map which we've marked as P930 [Realtime transcript read in error "P390"] for identification. I would ask you to do the following, and again, if you don't remember, that's fine, but what we're asking you to do is mark a line separating the VRS and the ABiH, the lines separating the ABiH and the HVO. If there are any point where there were HVO/VRS lines, please mark that. And some of these might not be visible on the map. That's fine. To the extent you can remember within the 3rd Corps area, mark the lines or where the units were of the 3rd Corps and the areas that they were responsible for. To the extent you know the units on the HVO side, which brigades were there, if you could mark those, if you recall. And if you recall or -- any of the VRS units that were on the opposite side of the ABiH with respect to these lines. I do note, Mr. President, page 89, line 10, should say P930, not P390. Now, General, is it clear what I'm asking you to do on this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll summarise. You have been asked to mark the VRS ABiH line on the map, then the ABiH HVO lines, the HVO VRS lines; if necessary, indicate the position of the 3rd Corps units, indicate the HVO unit positions, and to the extent that this is possible, indicate the position of the VRS units. This is quite clear, and it shouldn't be difficult to indicate these positions on the map to the extent that the witness can remember them. You have taken note of what have been requested of you. Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it's our mistake, because we were not able to check this, but could the Prosecution tell us what the scale of the map is and which area it covers. Does it cover all the municipalities that were covered by the 3rd Corps so -- because I don't think we have the entire map. Could they tell us about the dimensions of the map, or the scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, what is the scale of the map, and more importantly, does this map represent or cover the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps? In fact, the general will have a look now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's a 1:50.000 map covering the Central Bosnia area. And again, it's a map that we have used in this courtroom on several occasions. If the general has any comments, I welcome his contribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you had a quick look at the map. What would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've had a look at this map the scale of which is 1:50.000. It doesn't cover the entire zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. I can use this map and indicate the positions I've been asked to indicate to the extent that it's possible on this map. If I'm to inform the Chamber of everything that I can remember in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps on the 20th of June, 1993, then I would need a map the scale of which is 1:100.000. I have been given three tasks so I need three colours so that -- I need to be able to use three colours so I can depict this accurately. Otherwise, it will be confusing. Could these maps be put together? Because otherwise I won't be able to carry out my task. I need scissors, I need glue. This is a process that takes some time. If you asked an American general to do this I don't think he would be able to carry out the task in ten days' time. I'm trying to do my best, but if you bring an American general here and give him this task, well, I'll take my hat off to him if he actually manages to do it. I have been asked to do a lot here. I'll do my best because I want to contribute to the truth. There are 50 staff members who are involved in carrying out such a task, and bear this in mind. This is why I suggested I should do this here immediately, so that no one suggested that I use different means to carry out the task. But if you provide me with the equipment I need and the map or other maps, I'll do my best to mark all these locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, the only problem we have now is that the witness would prefer to have a map the scale of which is 1:100.000. The witness claims that the current map doesn't cover the entire area of the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility. Could we provide the witness with a map the scale of which is 1:100.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the large [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Switch to channel 7 to hear the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now it's back on 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Switch back to channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps the best course of action might simply be for us to discuss this with the Defence and the Chamber's legal officer and the representative of the Registry and to come up with a solution so that we're not debating this issue ad infinitum. If the witness wants a 1:100.000 map, we will endeavour to produce that for him to mark on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So it will be map 1 to 100.000 that is going to be provided to the witness, and the registrar is going to provide the witness with pencils in three colours. So among yourselves you are going to discuss this operation and how it can be carried out. It will be best if it could be done Monday morning just before the hearing. It would be more practical. General, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would also like the maps to be put together. I need more people who would put these maps together. There's no way I can finish that before Monday. Can I have a team of people? You must have a team of people who work here who could put these maps together. I don't have conditions for that in the hotel. My hotel room is very small. Do you know how big a desk I would need to put these maps before me? In my hotel room I have a small desk. Okay. I'll put the map on the bed, I will really try hard to do whatever I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rest assured you're not going to have to work in the hotel. You will work here. So rest assured you're not going to have to spend the entire weekend drawing lines on a map. On Monday morning you're going to have everything. The registrar will be here, the legal officer will be here, and we will deal with the problem, and we will save time. As we have already said, on Monday we will sit in the afternoon, on Tuesday we will sit in the morning, Thursday's also morning as well as the afternoon -- I'm sorry. On Wednesday also in the morning, Thursday morning, Thursday afternoon, Friday also in the morning. But if we finish on Thursday afternoon, there will -- there will not be any sitting on Friday. So in theory, you might have an additional sitting next week. So Monday afternoon, Tuesday morning, Wednesday morning, Thursday afternoon -- Wednesday afternoon, Thursday morning, Thursday afternoon, and if necessary, Friday morning, but we shall see. If everything goes well, maybe we won't have to sit in -- on Friday. We have added an additional session because we are going to have an additional afternoon. If there are no other pressing matters, we will deal with this issue of map immediately. General, of course you are not supposed to contact any of the parties. The only time you're going to be in the presence of any of the parties is when you're going to work on the material, which is going to happen on Monday in the course of the morning. The registrar is going to provide you with the necessary information. I wish you all a pleasant weekend, and we shall resume on Monday at quarter past two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
